usage: Korean summer's sticky heat that clings to your skin; very common July-August complaint
polite present; use when you walk outside and the air feels thick
한 attaches before a noun; describes the kind of day
-아/어서 reason form; lead-in to 'I turned on the AC'
examples: 장마철이라 그런지 방 안이 너무 후텁지근해요.
Maybe because it's monsoon season, the room is so muggy.
장마철 (rainy season) is when locals use this word most
밖에 나가자마자 후텁지근해서 바로 들어왔어요.
The moment I stepped outside it was so muggy that I came right back in.
captures the 'wall of humidity' feeling of a Korean summer
에어컨 좀 켜자, 후텁지근해서 잠이 안 와.
Let's turn on the AC, it's so muggy I can't sleep.
casual 반말 between friends or a couple at home
nuance: 후텁지근하다 is specifically hot AND humid at the same time — the heavy, sticky air of a Korean summer night. It's different from plain 덥다 (just hot); use it when the humidity makes the heat feel suffocating and your clothes stick to you.
mistakes: Using it for dry heat — if it's hot but not humid, say 덥다, not 후텁지근하다.
Spelling it 후덥지근하다; the standard spelling is 후텁지근하다.

usage: the brisk cool of early morning or late autumn; not freezing, just enough for a jacket
polite present; the go-to weather small talk in spring and fall
common phrase describing the daily temperature swing (일교차)
examples: 요즘 아침저녁으로 쌀쌀하니까 겉옷 챙기세요.
These days it's chilly morning and evening, so bring a jacket.
classic seasonal advice you'll hear and use constantly
오늘 좀 쌀쌀하지 않아요? 가디건 입고 올걸.
Isn't it a bit chilly today? I should've worn a cardigan.
natural office or cafe small talk
바람이 불어서 생각보다 쌀쌀하네요.
The wind's blowing so it's chillier than I expected.
-네요 for noticing/reacting in the moment
nuance: 쌀쌀하다 is a mild, brisk chill — the kind that makes you want a light jacket, typical of spring and autumn. It can also describe a person's cold, distant attitude (쌀쌀맞다 / 쌀쌀하게 대하다), so context tells you whether it's weather or personality.
mistakes: Using it for deep winter cold — that's 춥다 or 매섭다, not 쌀쌀하다.
Confusing it with 싸늘하다, which feels colder and often carries an eerie or tense undertone.

usage: gently warm, especially a winter day that's warmer than usual; also a soft, snug feeling
polite present; said happily when winter cold eases up
날(이) + adjective is a natural weather frame
examples: 오늘은 한겨울인데도 날이 포근하네요.
Even though it's midwinter, the day is so mild today.
the typical context: a surprisingly warm winter day
이불이 포근해서 일어나기 싫어요.
The blanket is so cozy I don't want to get up.
포근하다 also describes soft, snug things, not just weather
눈이 와도 바람이 없어서 포근한 느낌이에요.
Even though it's snowing, there's no wind so it feels cozy.
포근한 느낌 = a warm, gentle vibe
nuance: 포근하다 carries a warm, comforting feeling — mostly used for a winter day that turns out mild, or for soft, snuggly things like blankets. It's emotionally positive; you say it with relief or contentment, unlike neutral 따뜻하다.
mistakes: Using it for hot summer warmth — 포근하다 is for gentle/mild warmth, never summer heat.
Forgetting it also means 'soft and cozy' for objects; don't limit it to weather.

usage: ㅂ-irregular: stem changes before 어/으; intense, oppressive summer heat
the related noun you'll see in forecasts: 무더위가 계속되다
examples: 올여름은 유난히 무더워서 다들 힘들어해요.
This summer is unusually sweltering, so everyone's struggling.
유난히 = unusually; common summer complaint
무더운 날에는 수분 섭취가 정말 중요해요.
On sweltering days, staying hydrated is really important.
the kind of advice you hear on the news
밤에도 안 식어서 무더운 열대야가 계속돼요.
It doesn't cool down even at night, so the sweltering tropical nights continue.
열대야 (tropical night) pairs naturally with 무덥다
nuance: 무덥다 is stronger than 덥다 — it's heavy, oppressive heat, usually with humidity, that drains your energy. Note the ㅂ-irregular conjugation (무더워요, 무더운). The noun 무더위 appears constantly in summer weather reports.
mistakes: Conjugating it as 무덥어요; the correct ㅂ-irregular form is 무더워요.
Using it for mild warmth — 무덥다 is reserved for intense, draining heat.

usage: comfortable coolness, especially early autumn after summer heat breaks
polite present; said with relief when the weather turns nice
선선한 most often pairs with 바람 (breeze) or 날씨
examples: 이제 아침 공기가 선선해서 산책하기 딱 좋아요.
Now the morning air is pleasantly cool, perfect for a walk.
딱 좋다 = just right; classic early-autumn comment
밤바람이 선선하니까 창문 열어 둘게요.
The night breeze is nice and cool, so I'll leave the window open.
natural reason for opening a window
더위가 한풀 꺾이고 선선해졌네요.
The heat has died down a bit and it's gotten cool.
한풀 꺾이다 = (heat) to ease off; a very Korean expression
nuance: 선선하다 is a pleasant, refreshing coolness — the welcome relief you feel when summer ends and early autumn arrives. It's always positive, unlike 쌀쌀하다 (chilly enough to need a jacket) or 싸늘하다 (uncomfortably cold).
mistakes: Using it when it's actually cold — 선선하다 is comfortable, not chilly; for needing a jacket use 쌀쌀하다.
Pairing it with summer heat; 선선하다 implies the heat has already passed.

usage: bright, beautiful weather with blue skies; the ideal day for going out
화창한 + 날씨/봄날 are the typical pairings
examples: 오늘 날씨가 화창해서 한강 가기 딱 좋아요.
The weather's lovely and sunny today, perfect for going to the Han River.
화창한 날 = the day everyone heads to 한강
내일은 화창한 봄날이 될 거래요.
They say tomorrow will be a fine, sunny spring day.
-(이)래요 reporting the forecast
미세먼지도 없고 하늘이 화창하네요.
There's no fine dust and the sky is clear and sunny.
미세먼지 (fine dust) is a real daily concern in Korea
nuance: 화창하다 describes bright, clear, beautiful weather — sunny skies and a fresh feeling, the kind of day that lifts your mood. It's mostly used for spring and autumn 'perfect' days, and pairs naturally with 봄날 (spring day).
mistakes: Using it for merely 'not raining' — 화창하다 implies genuinely bright, pleasant weather, not just cloudy-dry.
Applying it to night; it describes daytime brightness.

usage: high moisture in the air; the defining feature of Korean summer and the rainy season
습한 before a noun; also 습한 공기 (damp air)
습하다 + 덥다 is the classic summer combo
examples: 장마철엔 너무 습해서 빨래가 잘 안 말라요.
During the rainy season it's so humid that laundry doesn't dry well.
a very real apartment-life problem in Korea
방이 습한 것 같아서 제습기를 틀었어요.
The room felt damp so I turned on the dehumidifier.
제습기 (dehumidifier) is a summer essential here
오늘은 습하지 않고 보송보송해서 좋네요.
Today's not humid and feels nice and dry — so pleasant.
보송보송하다 = pleasantly dry; the opposite feeling
nuance: 습하다 focuses on moisture/dampness in the air, separate from temperature — you can have a 습한 but cool day. In Korea it's the word behind summer misery: damp laundry, mold (곰팡이), and the constant hum of the 제습기.
mistakes: Confusing it with 덥다 (hot); 습하다 is about moisture, not heat, even if they often go together.
Using it for dry conditions — the opposite is 건조하다.

usage: low humidity in the air; the hallmark of Korean winter and spring
polite present; also used for dry skin (피부가 건조해요)
건조주의보 is a real warning issued in dry, fire-risk seasons
examples: 겨울엔 너무 건조해서 가습기를 꼭 틀어요.
In winter it's so dry that I always run a humidifier.
가습기 (humidifier) is a winter must-have in Korea
날씨가 건조해서 입술이 자꾸 트네요.
The weather's so dry my lips keep chapping.
트다 = (skin/lips) to chap; common winter complaint
피부가 건조할 땐 보습 크림을 발라요.
When my skin is dry, I put on moisturizing cream.
건조하다 applies to skin as well as air
nuance: 건조하다 is the dryness of low-humidity air, the opposite of 습하다 — typical of Korean winter and the spring fire-warning season. It applies equally to skin (피부가 건조하다) and can describe a dry, dull personality or tone, so let context guide you.
mistakes: Mixing it up with 습하다; 건조하다 = dry, 습하다 = humid.
Forgetting the skin/personality uses — it's not only a weather word.

usage: ㅂ-irregular; piercing winter cold or a sharp, cutting wind
매서운 바람/추위 are the standard pairings
examples: 바람이 매서워서 귀가 다 얼었어요.
The wind was so biting that my ears froze.
the visceral feeling of a Seoul winter wind
오늘 추위가 매서우니까 패딩 단단히 입으세요.
The cold is biting today, so bundle up well in your padded coat.
패딩 (padded coat) is the Korean winter uniform
한파에 칼바람까지 매섭게 불었어요.
On top of the cold wave, a knife-like wind blew bitterly.
칼바람 (knife wind) + 매섭다 is very natural
nuance: 매섭다 describes a fierce, piercing quality — most often a biting winter wind or sharp cold that hurts your skin. Note the ㅂ-irregular (매서워요, 매서운). It can also describe a sharp, severe gaze or scolding (매서운 눈빛), reflecting its core sense of 'cutting/intense'.
mistakes: Conjugating it as 매섭어요; the ㅂ-irregular form is 매서워요.
Using it for mild cold — 매섭다 is reserved for harsh, painful cold or wind.

usage: ㅂ-irregular; the soft, comforting warmth of sunshine
the natural subject is sunlight, not air temperature
examples: 봄 햇살이 따사로워서 벤치에 한참 앉아 있었어요.
The spring sunshine was so warm and gentle that I sat on the bench for a while.
the cozy feeling of basking in spring sun
창문으로 따사로운 볕이 들어와서 기분이 좋아요.
Gentle sunlight is coming through the window, so I feel good.
볕 = sunlight; 볕이 들다 = sun shines in
겨울인데도 햇살이 따사로워서 산책 나왔어요.
Even though it's winter, the sunshine is gentle and warm, so I came out for a walk.
often used to describe a sunny winter or spring afternoon
nuance: 따사롭다 is a softer, more poetic cousin of 따뜻하다, used almost exclusively for sunlight (햇살/햇볕) and warm feelings. It evokes a gentle, soothing warmth and a peaceful mood, so it's common in casual writing, captions, and heartfelt speech.
mistakes: Conjugating it as 따사롭어요; the ㅂ-irregular form is 따사로워요.
Using it for general air temperature — for that say 따뜻하다; 따사롭다 is mainly for sunshine.

usage: a sharper, colder chill than 쌀쌀하다; air that's gone genuinely cold
싸늘한 + 공기/날씨; also 분위기 (atmosphere) for a tense mood
-아/어지다; weather or a mood suddenly going cold
examples: 해가 지니까 공기가 갑자기 싸늘해졌어요.
Once the sun set, the air suddenly turned cold.
the chill that drops fast after sunset
새벽엔 꽤 싸늘하니까 따뜻하게 입고 나가세요.
It's quite cold at dawn, so dress warmly when you go out.
새벽 (dawn/predawn) is when it's coldest
내 농담에 분위기가 싸늘해졌어요.
My joke made the mood turn cold.
very common figurative use: an awkward, frozen atmosphere
nuance: 싸늘하다 is colder and sharper than 쌀쌀하다, often with an unsettling or tense edge. Beyond weather, Koreans use it constantly for a cold atmosphere — 분위기가 싸늘하다 means a room has gone awkwardly silent or frosty, like after a bad joke.
mistakes: Treating it as identical to 쌀쌀하다 — 싸늘하다 is colder and can feel eerie or tense.
Missing the figurative 'awkward atmosphere' use, which is extremely common in daily conversation.

usage: vivid idiom: heat so heavy the air feels steamed; standard spacing is 푹푹 찌다
pairs with 더위 (heat) for peak-summer days
examples: 요즘 날씨가 푹푹 쪄서 밖에 나가기 무서워요.
The weather's been boiling lately, so I'm scared to go outside.
everyday exaggeration locals use in a heat wave
에어컨 없이는 푹푹 찌는 여름을 못 버텨요.
Without AC, I can't survive the sweltering summer.
버티다 = to endure; relatable summer truth
삼복더위라 그런지 정말 푹푹 찌네요.
Maybe because it's the dog days of summer, it's really sweltering.
삼복더위 = the hottest stretch of summer (복날)
nuance: 푹푹 찌다 literally means '(the heat) steams you,' an idiomatic, very colloquial way to say it's brutally, oppressively hot — stronger and more expressive than 무덥다. Standard spelling spaces it as 푹푹 찌다, and you'll hear it everywhere during a Korean heat wave.
mistakes: Confusing 찌다 here with 찌다 'to gain weight' or 'to steam (food)' — context (날씨/더위) makes it 'sweltering'.
Writing it without the space; the standard form is 푹푹 찌다, not 푹푹찌다.
